result: The multipatcher is a robotic system capable of automatically obtaining blind whole-cell patch clamp recordings from multiple neurons simultaneously using four interacting electrodes in a coordinated fashion while avoiding mechanical coupling in the brain. The system was built by extending the autopatcher hardware and consists of four robotic arms with independent pressure control for each pipette.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C30-C33 collectively describe the multipatcher system's capabilities and hardware design. The experimental demonstrations throughout the paper (C7, C8, C23-C26) provide strong evidence that the system achieves its stated goals. The hardware descriptions are supported by detailed figures and component specifications.

result: In anesthetized mice, the multipatcher achieved dual or triple whole-cell recordings in 29% of trials and at least one whole-cell recording in 90% of trials. Individual pipettes had a 31.7% success rate for establishing whole-cell recordings, with 19% blockage rate, 57% gigaseal success, and 67.5% break-in success from gigasealed pipettes.
evaluation: Claims C7, C23-C24, and C53-C57 provide comprehensive quantitative performance metrics from 41 trials in 8 mice. The data is internally consistent (e.g., 52/164 = 31.7% overall success rate) and includes appropriate sample sizes. Statistical comparisons with prior work (C54) strengthen the evaluation.

result: In awake mice, the multipatcher obtained dual or triple whole-cell recordings in 18% of trials (17/97) and at least one recording in 55.7% of trials. Individual pipettes had a 17.3% success rate (67/388 pipettes), with 44.3% of trials yielding no usable recordings.
evaluation: Claims C8, C26, and C68-C74 provide detailed quantitative results from 97 trials in 32 awake mice. The lower success rates compared to anesthetized conditions are acknowledged and attributed to brain motion (C72). The data is internally consistent and sample sizes are adequate for the conclusions drawn.

result: Individual pipettes in the multipatcher maintained the same whole-cell yield (31%) as when working alone in the single autopatcher system, demonstrating that the multi-pipette coordination does not compromise individual pipette performance.
evaluation: Claims C25 and C57 provide a critical validation that the multipatcher does not reduce individual pipette performance. The 31.7% success rate per pipette (C57) matches the 31% rate when working alone (C25), supported by comparison with prior autopatcher work.

result: Initial attempts to scale up the autopatcher with synchronized operations showed very low yield (16.3% gigaseal success for waiting pipettes vs 36.8% for non-waiting). Tissue displacement from pipette motion and prolonged exposure to intracellular solution were identified as key problems, along with electrical noise from actuator movement.
evaluation: Claims C20-C22 and C34-C42 document the iterative development process and identify specific failure modes. The quantitative data (C34-C36, C39) from 19 trials clearly demonstrates the problems with the first algorithm iteration. The hypotheses about tissue displacement (C38, C40) are reasonable inferences from the resistance measurements.

result: The final algorithm iteration achieved a 58% gigaseal success rate (77/133 active pipettes), which was the highest yield among all three iterations and exceeded the success rate of the original single autopatcher algorithm.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 report the performance of the optimized algorithm from 41 trials. The 58% success rate represents a substantial improvement over the first iteration (22%) and is compared favorably to prior work. The data supports the conclusion that the interaction strategy was effective.

result: The multipatcher showed a decreased break-in success rate (67.5%, 52/77 gigasealed neurons) compared to the previous autopatcher study, with 6.4% of gigasealed neurons losing attachment while waiting and potential difficulty from increased holding duration at the gigaseal stage.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 acknowledge a limitation of the system with quantitative data. The 67.5% break-in rate (C60) is lower than prior work (C59), and potential explanations are offered (C61-C62). However, C62 notes this was not systematically explored, appropriately qualifying the speculation.

result: The multipatcher took an average of 10 minutes to obtain dual or triple recordings. In a subset of awake recordings involving anesthetic injection experiments, 41.2% of recorded neurons were lost due to increased motor activity following injection.
evaluation: Claims C6, C79-C80 provide timing and experimental condition details. The 10-minute average (C6) is a key performance metric. The loss of recordings due to motor activity (C80) is well-documented with quantitative data (14/34 neurons) and statistical analysis of motion indices, though this represents a specific experimental perturbation rather than typical awake recording conditions.

result: Once gigaseal or whole-cell configuration is achieved, the recording is remarkably stable against motion artifacts, enabling recordings in head-fixed and freely moving animals for extended durations (tens of minutes to hours for loose cell attached).
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 describe established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations to prior work. This background information justifies the algorithm design choice to prioritize achieving gigaseals quickly. The claims are appropriately attributed to prior literature.

result: The multipatcher requires increased installation time (3.2±0.3 min per pipette vs 2.0±0.4 min for autopatcher) due to positioning complexity. Theoretical scaling limits are 70 s/pipette operation time, with practical hardware limitations of 10-12 pipettes and non-linear increases in installation time.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 provide throughput analysis and scaling projections. The timing data (C89) is quantitative from 18 trials. The theoretical scaling calculation (C90) follows logically from the algorithm design. The hardware limitations (C91-C92) are reasonable engineering estimates based on physical constraints.

result: Traditional extracellular recordings and calcium imaging reveal supra-threshold spiking but cannot examine synaptic and subthreshold events important for understanding neuronal processes. While a few studies have performed simultaneous multi-neuron intracellular recordings in vivo, the difficulty of the technique limits its use.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C9-C16 establish the scientific context and motivation. These are well-established facts in neuroscience supported by appropriate citations (C10-C11, C15). The limitations of existing methods (C13, C16) and importance of subthreshold events (C14) are accurately stated and provide clear rationale for the work.

result: The autopatcher, previously developed by the authors, performs fully-automated whole-cell patch clamping of single neurons in the living mouse brain using pipette impedance measurements for neuron hunting followed by gigasealing and break-in with electronically controlled pressure regulators.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 describe prior work by the authors, appropriately cited (Kodandaramaiah et al., 2012, 2016). This background establishes the foundation for the multipatcher development and is necessary context for understanding the technical advances.

result: Whole-cell patch clamping is a gold standard electrophysiology tool that enables measurement of both suprathreshold spiking and subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations. Multi-neuron patching in brain slices has revealed insights into synaptic transmission and plasticity, but circuit-level interrogations have been difficult to perform in vivo, particularly in awake animals.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide established knowledge about patch clamping and its applications. C95 is supported by citation to prior work. These claims establish the scientific significance of the technical advance and are accurately stated.

result: The automation of multi-neuron recording opens possibilities for further parallelization and high-density mapping that would be difficult manually. Future improvements could include low-cost silicon amplifiers, imaging-based control, miniaturized manipulators (enabling 3-4 fold increases), novel electrode materials, and protocols for pipette reuse or robotic exchange.
evaluation: Claims C97-C107 are forward-looking statements about future possibilities and limitations. While some are supported by citations to relevant technologies (C99-C100, C105-C106), these are speculative projections rather than demonstrated results. The scaling estimates (C101) and limitations (C102-C104) are reasonable but not experimentally validated.

result: The multipatcher is a practical solution for performing intracellular recordings from multiple neurons in the intact brain.
evaluation: Claim C29 is a summary conclusion supported by the demonstrated performance metrics in both anesthetized (C7, C23-C24) and awake (C8, C26) conditions. The 29% and 18% success rates for multi-neuron recordings, combined with reasonable throughput (10 min average), support the practicality claim.

result: Key technical skills for surgery, durectomy, pipette pulling, solution preparation, and pressure control remain challenging and require time and practice to master, even with the automated system.
evaluation: Claim C108 provides an important caveat about the technical requirements for using the system, appropriately citing prior work. This is a reasonable statement about the limitations of automation and sets appropriate expectations for potential users.

result: All animal work was conducted in accordance with federal, state, and local regulations following NIH and AAALAC guidelines, with protocol #0113-008-16 approved by the MIT Institutional Committee on Animal Care.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 document ethical compliance and institutional approval. These are standard statements required for animal research and are appropriately included with specific protocol numbers.
